summary: This informational memo clarifies how the 32-bit IPv4 address space is interpreted in practice, since its meaning has changed a great deal since it was first defined. It describes the situation as it stood rather than defining a new standard.

plainLanguage.summary: House numbers once worked one way, but the town has grown and now people read them differently. This note explains the new reading.

questions: how is ipv4 address space used today
what is the difference between an ip address identifier and locator
how do nats change ipv4 addresses
why do ipv4 addresses not stay unique
subtitle: An IAB note on how NAT, private addresses, CIDR and renumbering changed what an IPv4 address means.

tldr.problem: The 32-bit IPv4 address was defined in 1981 as a unique, stable name for a host, but growth of the Internet changed what addresses really mean in practice.
tldr.mechanism: The note splits the address into two roles, identifier and locator, and shows that private address realms joined by NATs or ALGs weaken spatial uniqueness, while DHCP, PPP and renumbering weaken temporal uniqueness.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational snapshot, not a standard. It warns that addresses are no longer reliable identifiers and expects IPv6 to amplify that problem.

today: RFC 2101 is an Informational IAB note from February 1997 and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a snapshot of IPv4 address behavior at that time and does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Identifiers and Locators
sections.content:
The RFC says an address does two jobs. An identifier is a bit string used through a communication session to tell one host that the other end is truly the other end, for example in the TCP pseudo-header or in an IP Security association. A locator says where a packet must be delivered, and routing protocols treat IPv4 addresses as locators.

Identifiers must be unique among the hosts that communicate and must be valid for at least the lifetime of the communication. Locators must be unique within a routing realm (a set of inter-communicating routers) and valid only as long as routing needs them. In the traditional Internet one address served as both, and when the two uses conflicted, the locator use prevailed.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is both a name tag (who you are) and a map pin (where you are). The Internet cared more about the map pin, because a letter you cannot deliver is useless.

sections.title: The Ideal and the Reality
sections.content: Ideally identifiers are assigned at birth, never change and are never re-used, while locators describe the host's position in the topology and change whenever the topology changes. IPv4 addresses meet neither ideal. The RFC says the rest of the document is a snapshot of the real situation: addresses are no longer all globally unique and no longer all have indefinite lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: A perfect name never changes, and a perfect address changes whenever you move. A normal IPv4 address does neither job perfectly.

sections.title: Private Realms, NATs and ALGs
sections.content:
RFC 1918 lets corporate networks re-use part of the address space, forming multiple routing realms. Devices at realm boundaries range from application layer gateways (ALGs), which terminate the application data stream and must understand it, to network address translators (NATs), which only modify network and transport headers (including the pseudo-header checksum) and do not understand the application data.

A NAT cannot support applications that carry IP addresses at the application layer, such as FTP with the PORT or PASV command, but it can support anything else. An ALG supports only the applications coded into it. IP Security authentication assumes addresses are preserved end-to-end, and encryption hides the transport layer, so ALGs and NATs are likely to force a boundary between IP Security domains unless specific enhancements are designed. A site running a NAT or ALG probably needs two DNS servers, one inside and one outside, giving different answers to identical queries.

The RFC concludes that after RFC 1918 the spatial uniqueness of an address is not so much changed as split into multiple spaces, each a routing realm.
sections.plainLanguage: Many private towns now reuse the same house numbers. A translator at the town gate swaps numbers so mail can pass between towns, but it can confuse letters that mention a house number inside them.

sections.title: Addresses That Do Not Last
sections.content:
IPv4 blocks were for years assigned chronologically, effectively at random with respect to topology, so routing tables kept growing. Hierarchical routing with CIDR ([RFC 1518], [RFC 1519]) scales better, but it assumes allocation reflects topology. If a subscriber changes provider, it may need to renumber, and RFC 1900 shows why renumbering is increasingly frequent. DHCP and PPP also promote dynamic address allocation.

The result is that spatial uniqueness is largely preserved, so addresses still work as locators, but temporal uniqueness is no longer assured. An address may last for a time shorter than a TCP connection, so it is no longer a good identifier. The RFC says this affects end-to-end security and breaks TCP in its current form.

Multicast destinations can traverse a NAT. An anycast address can only be a locator, because it does not uniquely identify a host.
sections.plainLanguage: If your house number can change halfway through a phone call, the other person cannot rely on the number to know it is still you.

sections.title: Annex: From Classes to CIDR
sections.content:
IP addressing was first built around Class A, B and C network numbers. During 1992 and 1993 the Internet adopted Classless Inter-Domain Routing, which brings a new allocation architecture, new routing protocols and variable-size, contiguous, power-of-2 address blocks. Forwarding uses the longest-match algorithm, and BGP-4 aggregates routing information at the level of sites and providers.

The scaling gain depends on address allocation following topology. The annex notes that if no site that changes provider renumbered, the routing system might collapse under the volume of routing information. It also notes that allocation policy has evolved to add "address lending" as an alternative to "address ownership".
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses used to come in a few fixed sizes. Now they come in flexible sizes handed out by region, so one entry in a big map can cover a whole area.

sections.title: IPv6 and Security
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section only points to sections 4.1 and 5. Section 5 says the IPv6 model is very similar to the IPv4 state for temporal uniqueness, "only more so", because IPv6 will autoconfigure addresses and prefix changes are expected. IPv6 would therefore amplify the problem of finding stable identifiers for end-to-end security and session bindings such as TCP state.

The IAB says this is unfortunate and that the transition to IPv6 would be an ideal occasion to give upper-layer protocols temporally unique identifiers, which needs further study. For spatial uniqueness, the IPv6 address space is so big that a shortage requiring address translation is hardly conceivable.
sections.plainLanguage: The next kind of address will be even more likely to change, so the authors suggest inventing a separate, steady name tag for computers.

cells: Verifying the other end of a session
Telling where a packet must be delivered
At least the lifetime of the communication
Only as long as routing requires
Assigned at birth, never changes, never re-used
Describes position in topology, changes with it
